at: Heat and high rainfall lead to flooding of the coastal zone of South America, especially Peru and Ecuador and also the Pacific coast of Colombia and northern Chile
from_notes: Peru, Ecuador, coastal Colombia, N Chile | Heavy rain and flooding of the normally arid coast

source: PMF Physical Geography 06 p.49-51 (book p.413-415)

from_notes: Elnino current affects Indian climate.
x: El Nino in the Pacific weakens and delays India's monsoon, so it affects India's climate. The Gulf Stream, western intensification and the North Atlantic Oscillation are Atlantic features with no direct role.
source: NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC Exams 06 p.10 (book p.80)

from_notes: Unusual warm current (El Nino) flows southwards along the west coast of South America ... warms up ocean waters.
x: El Nino is the abnormal warming of the eastern tropical Pacific; La Nina is the opposite, cooling phase.
source: NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC Exams 06 p.14 (book p.84)

from_notes: The most prominent droughts in India have been El Nino droughts, including the recent ones (2014-16).
x: All three are correct: El Nino is a warm current off Peru in the eastern Pacific, its name means 'Christ child' because it appears around Christmas, and it contributed to India's 2014 monsoon deficit (about 12% below normal).
source: PMF Physical Geography 06 p.49-51 (book p.413-415); NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC Exams 06 p.14 (book p.84)

from_notes: Occurs approximately every 3 to 7 years.
x: El Nino recurs irregularly, about every 3-7 years, not every year. The other statements are true: it is a warm current off Peru, weakens the Indian monsoon, and La Nina strengthens it.
source: NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC Exams 06 p.14 (book p.84)

from_notes: El Niño is the name given to the occasional development of warm ocean surface waters along the coast of Ecuador and Peru.
x: El Nino is a Pacific Ocean phenomenon (off Peru and Ecuador), not an Indian Ocean or Bay of Bengal one.
source: PMF Physical Geography 06 p.49-51 (book p.413-415)

from_notes: El Niño is the name given to the occasional development of warm ocean surface waters along the coast of Ecuador and Peru.
x: El Nino develops in the eastern and central equatorial Pacific Ocean, off Peru and Ecuador.
source: PMF Physical Geography 06 p.49-51 (book p.413-415)

from_notes: The accumulation of warm water causes the thermocline to drop ... which cuts off the upwelling of cold deep ocean water along the coast of Peru.
x: Statement 1 is right: El Nino is a warm current off Peru. Statement 2 is wrong: the warm water cuts off the cold, nutrient-rich upwelling, so plankton and the fish catch fall, not rise.
source: PMF Physical Geography 06 p.49-51 (book p.413-415)

from_notes: Unusual warm current (El Nino) flows southwards along the west coast of South America ... Replaces the usual Peruvian cold current
x: El Nino is an abnormally warm ocean current that replaces the cold Peruvian current; it is oceanic, not an air mass, a wind or a low-pressure centre, though it affects the Indian monsoon.
source: NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC Exams 06 p.14 (book p.84)

from_notes: La Nina year ... monsoon winds, invigorating rains over
x: La Nina, the cool phase of ENSO, strengthens the trade winds and usually brings normal to above-normal monsoon rain to India. A positive IOD can also offset El Nino, but the Pacific opposite of El Nino is La Nina.
source: NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC Exams 06 p.10 (book p.80); PMF Physical Geography 06 p.51-52 (book p.415-416)

from_notes: North India winter | — | Colder, frequent cold waves (e.g. January 2012)
x: The January 2012 cold wave in north India was linked to La Nina, which brings colder winters and frequent cold waves to north India; El Nino, pollution and deforestation do not explain it.
source: app notes (old-notes.txt) 4:25 sub 1 (El Nino vs La Nina table)

from_notes: Indian monsoon | Weak, below normal (drought sign) | Normal to above normal
x: Both are wrong: La Nina is a cooling of the central/eastern equatorial Pacific, not the Indian Ocean, and it does affect the monsoon (it usually strengthens it).
source: PMF Physical Geography 06 p.49-51 (book p.413-415); NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC Exams 06 p.10 (book p.80)

from_notes: El Nino/ENSO and Indian monsoon are inversely related.
x: El Nino/ENSO and the Indian monsoon are inversely related: a strong El Nino means a weak monsoon.

from_notes: El Nino/ENSO phenomenon is closely monitored and is used for long-range forecasting
x: ENSO (El Nino and the Southern Oscillation) is used for short-term climate prediction and is associated with weak Indian monsoon years. La Nina usually brings good rain; jet streams and the greenhouse effect are not the event meant.
source: PMF Physical Geography 06 p.49-51 (book p.413-415); NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC Exams 06 p.14 (book p.84)

from_notes: Walker observed a correlation between high pressure over equatorial South Pacific and low pressure over equatorial South Indian Ocean, and vice versa.

source: NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC Exams 06 p.14 (book p.84)

x: All four are taken as correct (the usual key): El Nino comes at irregular 3-7-year intervals, carries warm water, its water is the warm, rain-freshened (less saline) western Pacific pool spreading east, and its atmospheric counterpart is the Southern Oscillation (ENSO).
source: PMF Physical Geography 06 p.49-51 (book p.413-415); ScienceDaily 30 Jan 2003 (sciencedaily.com/releases/2003/01/030130081105.htm: 'warmer temperatures and lower salinity in the western Pacific')

from_notes: The Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) is defined by the difference in sea surface temperature between two areas ... a western pole in the Arabian Sea (western Indian Ocean) and an eastern pole in the eastern Indian Ocean south of Indonesia.

from_notes: The water temperature must not fall below 68°F (20°C).
